result.summary: Pindar celebrates Xenokrates of Akragas' Pythian chariot victory, likening the ode to a treasure house at Delphi that no storm can destroy. He praises Xenokrates' son Thrasyboulos as a devoted son, comparing him to Antilochos, who died saving his father Nestor from Memnon.

scenes.title: The treasure house of song
scenes.summary: Pindar says the ode is a song-treasure at Apollo's valley for Xenokrates and Akragas, safe from storms, proclaiming the victory.
scenes.stakes: The victory's fame could be swept away like a treasure by storm, but the song will endure.

scenes.title: Cheiron's charge to Achilles
scenes.summary: Thrasyboulos keeps the precept that the centaur gave Achilles: honour Zeus and honour one's parents.

scenes.title: Antilochos dies for Nestor
scenes.summary: Antilochos saves his father Nestor from Memnon by dying in his place.
scenes.stakes: Antilochos risks death to save his father Nestor.

scenes.title: Praise of Thrasyboulos
scenes.summary: Pindar says Thrasyboulos matches the ancient example, uses wealth wisely, honours Poseidon and is a sweet host.

alias_notes.explanation: The centaur Cheiron, not named here, is identified by his mother Philyra.
Patronymic for Zeus, who is not named in this translation.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable image of the ode as a treasure house safe from storms.
Sweet closing image of hospitality, sweeter than honeycomb.

analysis.text: The ode links athletic victory with filial duty, using myth to show that honouring parents is a noble virtue.
Treasuries at Delphi held city offerings; Pindar's song-treasure image presents poetry as a lasting dedication.

fun_facts.text: This is among Pindar's earliest surviving poems, dated to 494 B.C.

language_notes.text: The "everlasting centre-stone" is the omphalos at Delphi, thought to mark the earth's centre; the "pilgrimage" is the journey to the Pythian games.
"Emmenidai" are the family of Emmenes, to which Theron and Xenokrates of Akragas belonged.
Krisa is the plain near Delphi where the Pythian chariot race was run.
"Son of Philyra" is the centaur Cheiron; "son of Peleas" is Achilles; "Kronos' son" is Zeus.
"Bought his father's flight by his own death" means Antilochos's death let Nestor escape.
"Our fathers' gauge" means the standard or measure set by the ancients.
"Pierides" are the Muses, so the phrase means learning and poetry.
"Earthshaker" is Poseidon, credited with creating the horse.

context_notes.text: Theron was the powerful tyrant of Akragas, a Sicilian city; Xenokrates won the chariot race.
Thrasyboulos is Xenokrates' son and charioteer, addressed here as the one who keeps the precept.
Antilochos, Nestor's son, fought at Troy; Memnon, king of the Ethiopians, came to help Troy.

literary_notes.text: Composing and travelling to sing is figured as ploughing the field of Aphrodite or the Graces, making song a cultivated harvest.
The ode is a built treasure house, suggesting lasting and guarded value, like offerings stored at Delphi.
The storm is compared to a fierce army born of the thunderous cloud, stressing how safe the song-treasure is.
Thrasyboulos's kindness is compared to honeycomb, ending the ode with sweetness and hospitality.
